tagline.text: San Juan's historic park honoring the first battle of the Philippine Revolution

location.label: Location
location.text: Pinaglabanan Street, San Juan, Metro Manila

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100–500 (including transport and snacks, per person for half a day)

children.text: Pinaglabanan Shrine is a national shrine park of about 5 hectares that commemorates the 1896 clash between the Katipunan and Spanish forces, the first battle of the Philippine Revolution. You can visit the Museo ng Katipunan and the Museo El Deposito, built over an underground reservoir, free of charge.

Pinaglabanan Shrine is a national shrine park on Pinaglabanan Street in San Juan, Metro Manila. It covers about 5 hectares and is jointly maintained by the City of San Juan and the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP). In late August 1896, Katipunan members led by Andrés Bonifacio attacked the Spanish powder magazine in what was then San Juan del Monte, and this is where that battle took place. It is regarded as the first major battle of the Philippine Revolution.

About 800 Katipuneros hoped to seize El Deposito, the reservoir that supplied water to Manila, and cut off the city's supply. They first took the powder magazine, but Spanish reinforcements arrived the next morning and turned the tide. Armed mostly with bolos, spears, and homemade guns, the Katipunan was badly defeated. The battle is a record of defeat rather than victory, yet Filipinos remember it as the day they first took up arms for independence. That is why the place name Pinaglabanan, meaning "place of the fight," became the name of the park. According to records, the Katipuneros gathered under Bonifacio and Emilio Jacinto from Mandaluyong and Sancho Valenzuela from Santa Mesa. The Spanish garrison had about 100 trained artillerymen and infantry with modern rifles, and after their commander was killed, the survivors withdrew to El Deposito. The next morning, General Bernardo Echaluce's Regiment 73 arrived and the situation reversed: about 153 Katipuneros were killed and about 200 captured, including Valenzuela. Some sources date the battle to August 29 and others to August 30, so this guide says late August.

At the center of the park stands the bronze sculpture Spirit of Pinaglabanan by Eduardo Castrillo, showing a woman and two children raising a bolo on a semicircular base. Walls on either side bear the names of Katipunan members believed to have taken part in the battle, and in front is an eternal flame symbolizing the nation's pledge to liberty. The site was declared a national shrine in 1973. Later, the San Juan city government and the Department of Public Works and Highways, in consultation with the NHCP, spent
on new flooring, landscaping, a perimeter fence, public toilets, LED lighting, and sprinklers, and the park reopened on November 25, 2019.

For travelers, this is not a flashy attraction but a quiet place to read modern Philippine history. The Museo ng Katipunan and Museo El Deposito inside the park are free, and because Greenhills Shopping Center is close, it pairs well with shopping as a half-day outing. Hours and booking rules can change, so check the latest announcements before you go.

This bronze sculpture by Eduardo Castrillo is the symbol of the park. It shows a woman and two children raising a bolo, and it is the spot most visitors photograph. A semicircular base stands behind the figures, so step back a little to fit the whole thing in the frame.

Walls on both sides of the monument carry the names of Katipunan members believed to have taken part in the 1896 battle, compiled from primary sources and published studies. As you walk slowly and read, you sense that the battle was the work of many ordinary people, not just a few heroes.

The eternal flame in front of the monument symbolizes the Filipino pledge to defend liberty. Wreath-laying ceremonies are sometimes held here on days such as Independence Day or the battle anniversary. Check the San Juan tourism office or NHCP announcements for the schedule.

This museum is run by the NHCP inside the park. It has old weapons and anting-anting amulets, copies of Katipunan documents, profiles of figures such as Gregoria de Jesus and Emilio Jacinto, and touch-screen explanations. A hologram display of Bonifacio reciting a poem has also been reported, so confirm the current exhibits on site.

This two-story museum stands above an underground reservoir built during the Spanish colonial era. It uses artifacts, photographs, scale models, and video to show how Manila's water supply developed, and after the upstairs galleries you go down to the underground reservoir. The underground section can feel cooler than outside, so it works well as a hot-afternoon stop.

This is the very reservoir that was the target of the 1896 battle. It has been restored and is open to the public, letting you see the geographic setting of the fighting. It was also used for military purposes during World War II.

The park, reopened in November 2019, has new flooring, landscaping, fencing, public toilets, LED lighting, and sprinklers. Its wide lawns and walkable paths make it a good place to rest after the museums. There are no restaurants inside the park, so bring snacks and water. The upgraded toilets and lighting also make it comfortable for families. If you come with children, use the lawn to rest and tell them the story of the battle.
Arrive at the park and start at the front with the Spirit of Pinaglabanan monument, the name walls, and the eternal flame. It is not yet hot, which is also good for photos.
Enter the Museo ng Katipunan to see the founding of the Katipunan, the background of the battle, and the exhibits on key figures. Reading the touch-screen explanations takes about
40 minutes

. If you first understand what the Katipunan was and why it led to armed revolt in August 1896, the scene in front of the monument will look different. Exhibit text may mix Filipino and English, so a translation app can help.
Move to the Museo El Deposito, view the upstairs galleries, and go down to the underground reservoir. The floor below may be wet, so wear comfortable shoes.
Leave the park and head toward Greenhills Shopping Center for lunch. There are no restaurants inside the park.
The museums are closed on Mondays and have at times required advance booking, so check the current arrangements with the NHCP or the San Juan tourism office before you leave.

items.title: Shopping combo route
items.subtitle: A full day of the shrine and Greenhills

children.text: See the monument and name walls, then visit the Museo ng Katipunan.
Tour the Museo El Deposito and the underground reservoir.
Take a taxi or Grab to Greenhills Shopping Center and have lunch.
Enjoy souvenirs and shopping at Greenhills, or continue on to Ortigas Center.
Museum closing times differ by source, so if you want to see them in the afternoon, put them early in the schedule.
Taking a Grab or taxi from Ninoy Aquino International Airport is the simplest way. Depending on traffic, it can take
40 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes
or more.
In a map app, search for "Pinaglabanan Shrine" or "Pinaglabanan Memorial Shrine."

items.title: By public transport from central Manila

children.text: One described route is to get off at MRT-3 Santolan-Annapolis Station and transfer to a jeepney or taxi. It may be too far to walk, so confirm locally.
Jeepneys from Camp Crame and RRCG buses on the Ortigas Avenue–Sta. Mesa route pass near the shrine.
If driving, head west on Bonny Serrano Avenue and pass Camp Crame, and the shrine will be on your right.
Roads get very congested at rush hour. Time your trip for daytime hours when the museums are open.
From Greenhills Shopping Center, it is easiest to take a taxi or Grab. Parking is reported to be available, but check the size and fees on site.
The dry season from November to May is best for seeing the outdoor park and the underground reservoir together. In the rainy season the lawns get wet and traffic builds up, so bring an umbrella.
Early morning or late afternoon is cooler and quieter. Around the late-August battle anniversary and June 12 Independence Day, wreath-laying ceremonies may be held and the crowds grow.

and may vary with local conditions.
There are no restaurants inside the park, so it is best to eat in nearby San Juan or Greenhills. Greenhills Shopping Center has a wide range of eateries and is convenient for lunch.
For lodging, hotels around Ortigas Center or Greenhills are a better choice than the area right at the shrine. Food and transport are close together there, which makes it easy to plan a day.
If you want to see the museums, go on a Tuesday to Sunday morning. They are known to be closed on Mondays, so check before you visit.
There have been notices that NHCP museums accept advance reservations or ask you to call ahead. Groups should always contact them in advance.
The phone numbers +63 2 576 4336 and 385 5896 have been listed for the Museo ng Katipunan, but numbers can change, so verify the latest one.
Combining Greenhills Shopping Center and Ortigas Center into a half-day plan cuts down on travel.
Photography is generally allowed, but check the rules inside the museum galleries.
The underground reservoir can be damp and slippery, so low-heeled shoes are best.
The park has security staff, but keep your belongings on you during quiet hours.
Reading up on the history beforehand makes the exhibits much more interesting. Try searching for the 1896 Katipunan uprising and Andrés Bonifacio.
Some audio guides at the Museo El Deposito are reported to require logging in to an app, so check your data and battery.
Museum hours and booking rules differ by source and change often. Check the latest announcements from the NHCP or the San Juan tourism office before you go.
Opening hours are listed variously as Tuesday to Sunday, from 8:00 or 9:00 AM to 4:00 or 5:00 PM, depending on the source. Arrive before 3:00 PM so you can get in before closing.
Roads around Bonny Serrano Avenue can be congested at rush hour, so allow plenty of travel time.
There are no restaurants in the park and some areas have little shade, so bring water and a hat during the day.
On days with commemorative events, some areas may be closed off.
As this is a revolution memorial, do not climb on the monument or make noise near the eternal flame.
Close to the shrine and good for combining lunch and shopping. Travel time depends on traffic, so confirm locally.
A business and shopping district east of San Juan with many hotels and restaurants.
A large mall on the Ortigas side with convenient transport.
